Neonatal body mass in the Dusky rat has been estimated from data on the closely related black rat, with newborns weighing approximately 4.55 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.55 grams]. This modest initial mass is typical of altricial murid rodents, which are born hairless and with closed eyes, requiring an extended period of maternal care before they become independent. Under standard thermoneutral conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation period in this species is about 22 days [tg = about 22 days], a value that falls within the range reported for other Rattus species of comparable body size. This relatively short gestation is followed by a developmental phase during which the young grow rapidly, relying exclusively on maternal milk. The ultimate wet weight for adult females, representing the maximum body mass attained by mature individuals, reaches approximately 213 grams [Wwi = approximately 213 grams], though field-caught specimens often range between 22 and 213 grams depending on local resource availability and seasonal conditions. This considerable variation in body size reflects the species' ability to capitalise on pulsed food resources in its floodplain habitat, with heavier individuals typically recorded during periods of high primary productivity.

The timing of weaning marks a critical transition from nutritional dependence on the mother to independent foraging, and in the Dusky rat this milestone occurs at 26 days after birth [tx = 26 days after birth], a value inferred from life-history patterns in Rattus rattus at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. When measured under standard laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], weaning coincides with the eruption of the first molars and the onset of solid food consumption, though the young may continue to suckle intermittently for several days thereafter. Following weaning, the pre-reproductive juvenile stage is characterised by rapid somatic growth and the gradual accumulation of fat reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of future reproduction. The period between birth and the attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is estimated at 90 days after birth [tp = 90 days after birth] when animals are maintained at 37.5 °C at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively early maturation is consistent with the species' position along the fast end of the life-history continuum, allowing individuals to begin contributing to population growth within a single breeding season in the seasonally unpredictable wetlands of northern Australia where the Dusky rat is endemic.

Reproductive output in this species is strongly influenced by the boom-bust dynamics of its floodplain environment. Females typically produce litters of nine pups [N_R_i = litters of nine pups] during each breeding event, and they are capable of producing approximately three litters per year [F_R_i = approximately three litters per year] under favourable conditions, yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate that allows rapid population recovery following dry-season contractions. This high fecundity is a classic demographic strategy among small mammals inhabiting unpredictable environments, where the ability to convert ephemeral resource pulses into offspring quickly is strongly favoured by natural selection. The maximum lifespan of the Dusky rat is estimated at about 4.2 years [am = about 4.2 years] based on data from Rattus rattus, though individuals in the wild rarely survive more than one or two breeding seasons due to intense predation pressure and the extreme seasonal flooding events that characterise their habitat at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Under controlled captive conditions maintained at 37.5 °C, however, individuals have been documented to persist for as long as 1,533 days, underscoring the species' potential longevity when extrinsic mortality risks are removed.

Basal metabolic rate in the Dusky rat has been measured at 123 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 123 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when assessed under resting conditions at the species' preferred body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This metabolic value is relatively high for a mammal of this body size, reflecting the species' active lifestyle and the energetic demands of thermoregulation in the seasonally variable tropical environment it inhabits. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, non-reproductive adults resting during their inactive phase, ensuring that the recorded oxygen consumption genuinely represents the minimal energetic cost of maintenance. For comparison, this rate is approximately 30 percent higher than that predicted by allometric equations for a 213-gram rodent, suggesting that the Dusky rat possesses an elevated metabolism that may be linked to its high reproductive output and short generation time. The thermal regime at which these measurements were taken is critical, as metabolic rate in small endotherms is highly sensitive to ambient temperature, and deviations from thermoneutrality can inflate energy expenditure substantially.

Ecologically, the Dusky rat occupies a narrow niche along the coastal floodplains of the Northern Territory, where its life history is finely tuned to the alternating wet and dry seasons. During the wet season, when grasses and sedges produce abundant seeds and invertebrates flourish, females can initiate breeding almost immediately after reaching puberty at 90 days after birth. The weaning period of 26 days after birth is synchronised with peak food availability, maximising juvenile survival. The ultimate body mass of 213 grams for females is rarely attained during dry-season conditions, when food is scarce and individuals must rely on stored fat reserves to survive until the next monsoon. Body mass at birth remains consistently around 4.55 grams, suggesting that neonatal size is canalised despite the considerable variation in maternal condition. Population density fluctuates dramatically, with numbers increasing several hundred-fold during wet-season irruptions, only to crash during the dry-season when the floodplains desiccate and refugial habitats become severely limited. This boom-bust dynamic is one of the best-documented examples of extreme population fluctuation in an Australian rodent.
